title: Trees: Right Side View
oneLiner: List the nodes you would see looking at a tree from the right: the last node of each level in a level-order (BFS) traversal.
keyTakeaway: The right side view is the last node of every level. Run level-order BFS, processing one level at a time (take the queue's size before the loop), and record the last node you dequeue in each level. O(n) time, O(n) queue space. A DFS that visits right before left and records the first node at each new depth gives the same answer.
explanation:
Imagine standing to the right of a binary tree. Return the values you can see, top to bottom. For [1, 2, 3, null, 5, null, 4] that is [1, 3, 4]. Careful: it is not just the rightmost branch. In [1, 2, 3, 4] the bottom level has only 4, on the left, and it is still visible: the answer is [1, 3, 4].

"One answer per level" means level-order traversal, which you met in Binary Tree Level-Order Traversal. Put the root in a queue. While the queue is not empty, read its current size, which is exactly the number of nodes on this level, and dequeue that many nodes, enqueueing their children. The last node you dequeue in that batch is the rightmost node of the level, so add its value to the answer.

The DFS alternative is just as short: recurse with a depth, visiting the right child before the left, and whenever depth equals the answer's length you are the first node seen at a new depth, which from the right is the visible one. It uses O(h) stack instead of a queue as wide as a level.

Both visit every node once: O(n). The BFS queue holds at most one level, up to about n/2 nodes for a full tree, so O(n) space. The same "take the size, process one level" loop answers level averages, the largest value in each row, zigzag order and minimum depth.

The visualization runs BFS on [1, 2, 3, null, 5, null, 4] and highlights each level's last node.

pythonHarnessPreamble:
null = None

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def build_level_order_tree(values):
    # Builds a tree from a level-order list; null (None) marks a missing child.
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(values[0])
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    i = 1
    while head < len(queue) and i < len(values):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if values[i] is not None:
            node.left = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(values) and values[i] is not None:
            node.right = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root

def tree_to_list(root):
    # The tree as a level-order list with None for missing children, trailing Nones trimmed.
    result = []
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if node is None:
            result.append(None)
            continue
        result.append(node.val)
        queue.append(node.left)
        queue.append(node.right)
    while result and result[-1] is None:
        result.pop()
    return result
recognitionSignals: One value per depth: the rightmost, leftmost, largest, average of each level.
"View from the side" or "visible from the right".
gotchas: Following only right children misses levels whose last node sits in the left subtree.
Without snapshotting the queue size at the start of each level, levels blur together.
Return [] for an empty tree instead of enqueueing null.
confusableWith: Binary Tree Level-Order Traversal returns every node grouped by level; this keeps one per level.
Invert a Binary Tree also touches every node, but changes the tree instead of reading it level by level.

complexity.note: Every node is enqueued and dequeued once. The queue holds at most one level, which is up to about n/2 nodes in a full tree. (The right-first DFS version needs O(h) stack instead.)
